title: Query Store
description: Leverage Query Store to track query performance over time, identify regressions, and force optimal query plans.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **Query Store**. Leverage Query Store to track query performance over time, identify regressions, and force optimal query plans. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of Query Store and be confident in applying it to your projects.

blocks.text: Query Store is a SQL Server feature that automatically captures query execution history, tracks plan changes over time, and provides a persistent store of query performance data. Unlike the plan cache, which loses history on restarts or eviction, Query Store retains performance data in user-managed tables, enabling long-term trend analysis and plan regression detection.

blocks.title: Query Store Is Essential
blocks.text: Starting with SQL Server 2016, Query Store should be enabled on every production database. It is the most effective tool for answering the question: 'Why did this query suddenly get slow?'

Query Store captures queries and their execution plans during normal operation. It stores this data in internal tables within the database, partitioned by time. Each query has a query_id, and each plan has a plan_id. Performance metrics — duration, CPU, memory, I/O — are tracked for each plan over time.

terms.definition: A unique identifier for a query text string within Query Store. Identical text maps to the same query_id.
A unique identifier for an execution plan associated with a query_id. Different plans for the same query have different plan_ids.
Performance metrics collected per plan_id per time interval, including average duration, CPU time, logical reads, and execution count.
A mechanism to pin a specific execution plan to a query, forcing SQL Server to use it regardless of what the optimizer would otherwise choose.
When a query's performance degrades because SQL Server switched to a slower execution plan, typically due to statistics changes or cardinality estimate shifts.

blocks.text: Query Store is disabled by default. Enable it at the database level with ALTER DATABASE. You can configure the capture mode to ALL, AUTO, or NONE, and set retention policies for how long data is kept.

blocks.title: Configuring Query Store
blocks.code:
-- Enable Query Store for a database
ALTER DATABASE [AdventureWorks]
SET QUERY_STORE = ON;

-- Configure Query Store options
ALTER DATABASE [AdventureWorks]
SET QUERY_STORE (
    OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE,
    CLEANUP_POLICY = (STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 30),
    DATA_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 900,
    MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB = 5000,
    QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO,
    MAX_PLANS_PER_QUERY = 200
);

-- Verify Query Store status
SELECT 
    name AS database_name,
    is_query_store_on,
    query_store_capture_mode,
    query_store_flush_interval_seconds,
    max_storage_size_mb
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = 'AdventureWorks';

blocks.text: SSMS provides built-in Query Store reports accessible via the database's Query Store folder in Object Explorer. The most valuable reports are: Top Resource Consuming Queries, Regressed Queries, Queries With Forced Plans, and Query Wait Statistics. These reports help you quickly identify performance problems and trends.

blocks.title: Core Query Store Reports
items: Regressed Queries — queries whose performance has degraded since their previous execution
Top Resource Consuming Queries — queries ranked by duration, CPU, memory, or I/O
Queries With Forced Plans — queries currently using a forced execution plan
Query Wait Statistics — time spent waiting for resources broken down by wait type

blocks.text: A plan regression occurs when SQL Server switches to a slower plan for a query that previously ran efficiently. Query Store makes regressions visible by tracking multiple plans per query and their associated performance metrics. When a regression is detected, you can force the previous good plan to restore performance immediately while investigating the root cause.

blocks.title: Force a Plan with T-SQL
Forcing Plans Is Temporary
blocks.text: Forcing a plan restores performance immediately but masks the root cause. Always investigate why the optimizer chose a different plan — typically stale statistics or parameter sniffing. Resolve the underlying issue and then unforce the plan.

blocks.caption: How Query Store detects a plan regression and enables forced plan recovery.
blocks.definition:
flowchart LR
    A[Query Executes] --> B[New Plan Generated]
    B --> C[Query Store Records Plan]
    C --> D[Compare to Previous Plans]
    D -->|Performance Degraded| E[Regression Detected]
    E --> F[Force Previous Good Plan]
    F --> G[Performance Restored]
    D -->|Performance OK| H[Continue]

blocks.text: Query Store exposes its data through a set of catalog views in the database. The core views are sys.query_store_query, sys.query_store_plan, sys.query_store_runtime_stats, and sys.query_store_wait_stats. You can query these views to build custom performance dashboards and alerts.

blocks.title: Query Store Custom Report
blocks.code:
SELECT 
    qt.query_sql_text,
    q.query_id,
    p.plan_id,
    rs.avg_duration / 1000.0 AS avg_duration_ms,
    rs.avg_cpu_time / 1000.0 AS avg_cpu_ms,
    rs.avg_logical_io_reads,
    rs.execution_type_desc,
    CONVERT(DATE, rs.last_execution_time) AS stat_date
FROM sys.query_store_query_text AS qt
INNER JOIN sys.query_store_query AS q ON qt.query_text_id = q.query_text_id
INNER JOIN sys.query_store_plan AS p ON q.query_id = p.query_id
INNER JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats AS rs ON p.plan_id = rs.plan_id
WHERE CONVERT(DATE, rs.last_execution_time) >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, GETDATE())
ORDER BY rs.avg_duration DESC;

items: Enable Query Store on all production databases at the READ_WRITE operational mode
Set an appropriate MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB to retain at least 30 days of history
Monitor the Query Store size and clean up unnecessary data with sp_query_store_force_plan cleanup
Use forced plans as a temporary fix, not a permanent solution
Review regressed queries weekly and investigate root causes
Combine Query Store data with execution plan analysis for complete diagnosis

blocks.title: Detect and Resolve a Plan Regression
blocks.description: Simulate a plan regression by updating statistics on a table, then use Query Store to identify the regression and force the original plan.
steps: Enable Query Store on your test database with READ_WRITE mode
Run a complex query multiple times and capture the plan_id from Query Store
Update statistics on the underlying table with FULLSCAN to trigger a plan change
Run the same query again and observe a new plan_id with different performance metrics
Query Query Store to compare the old and new plans side by side
Force the original good plan using sp_query_store_force_plan
Run the query again to confirm performance is restored
Document the root cause (statistics change) and create a fix strategy
blocks.expectedOutcome: You will have detected a plan regression, forced a good plan, and understood the relationship between statistics changes and plan quality.

items.question: Does Query Store add significant overhead?
items.answer: No. Query Store is designed for minimal overhead. The default configuration (AUTO capture, 900-second flush interval) adds less than 1% overhead for most workloads. You can tune the DATA_FLUSH_INTERVAL_SECONDS if needed.

items.question: Can I use Query Store on Azure SQL Database?
items.answer: Yes. Query Store is fully supported on Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance. The configuration options and catalog views are identical to on-premises SQL Server.

items.question: What happens when Query Store storage fills up?
items.answer: Query Store automatically switches to READ_ONLY mode when the MAX_STORAGE_SIZE_MB limit is reached, stopping new data capture. Increase the size limit or reduce the STALE_QUERY_THRESHOLD_DAYS to continue capturing.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: Query Store captures query execution history persistently, surviving server restarts and plan cache evictions
Enable it on all production databases — it is essential for diagnosing plan regressions
Use built-in reports to identify regressed queries and top resource consumers
Forced plans provide immediate relief for regressions while you investigate root causes
Catalog views enable custom monitoring, alerting, and historical trend analysis

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid
Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **Query Store**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of Query Store when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Comprehensive Code Example

This example demonstrates a production-ready implementation of **Query Store**. Study the code carefully, paying attention to error handling, type safety, and best practices. Try running it yourself and experiment with variations to deepen your understanding.

data.title: Production-Ready Implementation: Query Store
data.content: Complete working example demonstrating best practices and common patterns.
data.code:
-- SQL Example with Best Practices
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(o.order_total) AS total_spent,
    AVG(o.order_total) AS average_order
FROM 
    sales.customers c
LEFT JOIN 
    sales.orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date >= DATEADD(year, -1, GETDATE())
WHERE 
    c.is_active = 1
    AND c.created_date >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email
HAVING 
    COUNT(o.order_id) > 0
ORDER BY 
    total_spent DESC
OPTION 
    (RECOMPILE);

-- Performance Tips:
-- 1. Use appropriate indexes on join columns
-- 2. Avoid SELECT * - specify only needed columns
-- 3. Filter early with WHERE clause
-- 4. Use JOINs instead of subqueries when possible

data.text: Performance Considerations
Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **Query Store**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **Query Store**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
